The primary objective of this project was to create a genomic library using a streptomycin-resistant strain of E.coli Top10 (4537 bp) as the genomic DNA, incorporating it into a pUC19 plasmid (2686 bp) vector. The successful construction of this genomic library was expected to confer streptomycin resistance to a recipient E.coli strain Mach1 through the functional selection of the rspL gene. However, throughout the experiment, several challenges were encountered, leading to changes in the experimental design and troubleshooting of errors.

An initial gel electrophoresis performed to confirm the presence of the rspL gene after digestion of genomic DNA with BamHI resulted in no visible bands. This was primarily due to the low concentration of the originally isolated genomic Top10 DNA (33.2 ng/µL), which was further diluted during the digestion reaction and loading of the gel. This concentration was below the minimum detection limit required for the INtRON RedSafeTM nucleic acid stain to work efficiently (50 ng/µL). As a consequence, no bands were detected, and the experiment had to be repeated with a new and cleaned up genomic DNA sample.

Subsequent gel electrophoresis performed after digesting the cleaned-up genomic DNA with BamHI showed successful digestion of the genomic Top10 DNA, as evidenced by a shorter smear in comparison to the uncut band of the genomic DNA. In addition, the plasmid pUC19 showed two very faint bands after digestion with BamHI, indicating appropriate digestion of the plasmid as well.

A ligation reaction was set up using a 1:1 ratio for cut genomic Top10 DNA (insert) and cut plasmid pUC19 (vector). After overnight incubation at 4 °C, the ligated product was transformed into Mach1 chemically competent cells. The initial transformation results were inconclusive due to contamination observed in the positive control plate. A second transformation attempt also resulted in inefficient uptake of DNA by the host organism, leading to an unsuccessful transformation.

To increase the likelihood of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene, a third gel electrophoresis was performed using HindIII in addition to BamHI for digesting both genomic Top10 DNA and plasmid pUC19. The use of two different enzymes would increase the accuracy of the construct and facilitate the incorporation of the desired fragment into the plasmid.

Based on the information provided by the restriction analyzer, the BamHI enzyme cuts at two different sites on genomic DNA (180 and 2865), producing large fragments that appeared as a smear in the gel electrophoresis images. HindIII was introduced to cut at an additional site (4130) on genomic DNA, increasing the likelihood that the fragment containing the rspL gene would be successfully incorporated into the plasmid.

In summary, the construction of a genomic library using E.coli Top10 genomic DNA and pUC19 plasmid DNA encountered several challenges throughout the experiment, including low DNA concentrations, contamination, and inefficient transformation. The introduction of the HindIII enzyme in addition to BamHI for restriction digestion was expected to increase the probability of obtaining a fragment containing the rspL gene. Further optimization of ligation and transformation protocols may be necessary to enhance the efficiency of the genomic library construction and subsequent functional selection of the streptomycin resistance-conferring rspL gene. Predictive data analytics has become increasingly important in supply chain demand forecasting, as it offers various benefits such as improved operational efficiency, cost reduction, and enhanced decision-making. The application of big data analytics and machine learning technologies has revolutionized the way supply chain management activities are conducted, enabling organizations to better anticipate and react to changes in market dynamics. This literature review focuses on recent research findings that demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of predictive data analytics in supply chain demand forecasting.

In recent studies, researchers have highlighted the potential of big data and predictive analytics in improving the social and environmental sustainability of supply chains (Dubey et al., 2019). Implementing big data solutions and making use of real-time key performance indicators (KPIs) of the supply chain enables companies to evaluate their operations within a dynamic system (Dev et al., 2019).

Furthermore, advancements in analytics and machine learning have led to the development of novel approaches such as Poly-linear Regression with Augmented Long Short Term Memory Neural Network (PLR-ALSTM-NN) (Ahmed et al., 2022). This model, based on deep learning, has been shown to predict future financial market trends more effectively than traditional neural networks and machine learning tools.

Another area of interest is the integration of information and communication technologies (ICT) with big data analytics and blockchain technologies to create next-generation agricultural marketing systems in India (Shrivastava & Pal, 2019). The proposed framework comprises functionalities such as Market Intelligence, Food Supply Chain, and One Stop Mobile App, with the aim of facilitating better decision-making for farmers and improving overall supply chain efficiency.

The use of machine learning algorithms for stock price prediction has also been investigated (Wang, 2021). Although predicting stock prices remains a challenging task due to the presence of numerous influencing factors, the application of high-level machine learning models such as auto-ARIMA, Prophet, and LSTM demonstrates the potential for more accurate predictions.

Moreover, the implementation of digital twins in supply chain networks enables data-driven, real-time decision-making and improved resilience (Kulaç et al., 2022). By providing a digital replica of a supply chain system, digital twins can help organizations monitor operations, perform predictive analytics, and optimize their processes.

Potential Approaches to Overcome Human Resource Challenges in Green Air
In the context of GA’s current situation, some core HRM concepts and contemporary practices that can be critically assessed include employee motivation theories, stakeholder theory, workforce diversity and inclusion, recruitment and hiring strategies, and employee engagement and well-being.
One aspect of motivation theories that can be applied to GA’s problems is the expectancy theory by Fudge and Schlacter (1999). This theory suggests that employees are driven to act in a certain way based on the expectation that their efforts will lead to a desired outcome, and this outcome will be rewarding. In the case of GA, the company can use the expectancy theory to increase the motivation of employees by clarifying expectations and establishing a strong connection between individual and organizational goals. This approach may help GA to temporarily maintain employee motivation while they work on improving the compensation packages.
Another core HRM concept relevant to GA’s situation is stakeholder theory, which highlights the need for organizations to manage relationships with various stakeholders effectively (Thornock, 2016). In GA’s case, the relationship with trade unions has been challenging due to conflicts over pay and working conditions. These tensions could have been better managed through a more proactive approach to communication, negotiation, and conflict resolution involving all relevant stakeholders.
The concept of diversity and inclusion in the workplace is also critical for GA. Due to the mixed fleet crews, employees with different levels of experience, contracts, and backgrounds are working together, which could lead to conflicts or misunderstandings. It is essential for GA to foster an inclusive work environment that acknowledges and accommodates employees’ differences while promoting a sense of belonging and collaboration.
A relevant contemporary HR practice for GA is developing a strong recruitment and hiring strategy. As GA faces potential workforce shortages, they will need a comprehensive plan to attract and retain qualified employees with skills that match the organization’s needs. This recruitment strategy could include targeted job postings, campus hiring, increased employee referrals, and the use of technology such as social media and online job portals. GA could also consider offering competitive training programs and development opportunities to entice prospective employees.
Finally, employee engagement and well-being should be a top priority for GA’s HR team. The current low morale and dissatisfaction among employees is affecting the quality of service provided to customers, further damaging the company’s public image. GA needs to engage its employees by addressing their concerns, providing support, and creating an environment that promotes a healthy work-life balance. Such efforts can improve employee satisfaction, increase productivity, and thus boost the organization’s overall performance.
In sum, GA’s HR team should critically assess and implement appropriate HRM concepts and contemporary practices to address the critical issues of employee motivation, stakeholder relations, workforce diversity and inclusion, recruitment and hiring, and employee engagement and well-being. By proactively addressing these challenges, GA can create a positive work environment that ultimately leads to improved organizational performance and customer satisfaction.

Recommended Solutions
In light of the aforementioned HR issues faced by GA, several recommended solutions can be proposed to help the airline address its current challenges, improve employee morale, and strengthen its public image.
First and foremost, GA should consider engaging in open and transparent dialogue with its employees and the trade unions representing them. Maintaining strong communication channels, actively listening to employees’ concerns, and being transparent about the organization’s goals and challenges can help build trust and facilitate constructive negotiations (Baraldi and Radaelli, 2020). Collaborative problem-solving efforts with trade unions can lead to mutually beneficial agreements on issues such as pay, working conditions, and employment contracts, ultimately fostering a positive work environment.
Revisiting GA’s compensation packages is another solution that merits consideration. While the current financial situation may prevent immediate changes to employee compensation, GA could develop a comprehensive plan outlining adjustments to be made once the organization’s financial health improves (Purcell and Hutchinson, 2007). This strategy may include offering more competitive salaries or restoring some of the benefits and rewards that employees previously enjoyed. By presenting a well-defined plan for the future, GA can regain its employees’ trust and reinforce commitment to the organization.
Additionally, GA should consider implementing measures that promote employee engagement and overall well-being. This may involve offering greater flexibility with working hours, ensuring that employees have a healthy work-life balance, and providing resources for mental and physical health support (Kahn, 1990). By fostering a supportive work environment, GA can improve employee morale, reduce absenteeism, and enhance productivity.
To address the potential workforce shortage and recruitment challenges, GA needs to develop a strategic approach to recruiting and retaining talent. Armstrong and Taylor (2020) suggest adopting a multifaceted recruitment strategy that incorporates targeted job postings, partnerships with educational institutions, employee referral programs, and the utilization of social media and online platforms. Additionally, offering continuous learning, development, and growth opportunities within the organization can make GA a more attractive employer, ultimately aiding in the recruitment of new employees.
Lastly, GA should strive to improve its public perception by delivering exceptional customer service and addressing customer complaints efficiently. To achieve this goal, the organization must invest in training and development programs aimed at enhancing employees’ customer service skills (Zeithaml et al., 2006). Empowered and motivated employees are more likely to contribute to an improved customer experience which, in turn, can positively impact GA’s public image.
In conclusion, by implementing these recommendations, GA can address its HR challenges, improve employee morale, and enhance its public reputation, paving the way for organizational success and growth in an increasingly competitive market.

Conclusion
In conclusion, the challenges faced by GA highlight the critical role of effective human resource management in maintaining employee satisfaction, fostering a positive work environment, and sustaining a competitive edge. Through open communication and collaboration with trade unions, revisiting compensation plans, promoting employee engagement and well-being, adopting strategic recruitment approaches, and investing in customer service training, GA can address the multifaceted issues that currently affect the organization. By proactively tackling these challenges and prioritizing the well-being and satisfaction of its employees, GA can pave the way for success in an increasingly competitive market while enhancing its public image and solidifying its position as a leading global airline.

The use of sales promotion strategies, a wide range of tactics and techniques designed to stimulate customer interest and increase sales of products or services, has become increasingly important for organizations as they seek to improve their performance in today’s highly competitive business environment (Kotler et al., 2017). The proposed study seeks to explore the effect of sales promotion strategies on the overall performance of Nigeria Breweries Limited (NBL), a leading brewing company in Nigeria’s beverage industry. The research is of great significance due to the ever-growing competitive landscape of the beverage industry, where companies compete on several fronts, including product quality, branding, and promotional activities. It aims to fill an existing knowledge gap by evaluating the effectiveness of sales promotion strategies and their ethical implications, consequently providing actionable insights on adopting innovative tactics and training programs.
From a theoretical perspective, this research will draw on marketing theories. The consumer behavior theory, according to Hanaysha (2016), posits that individuals and groups make consumption decisions based on their needs, preferences, and the perceived values of available options. The stimulus-response theory, on the other hand, contends that consumers will react to a promotional stimulus, such as discounts or freebies if the perceived results align with their needs and elicited affect. Finally, the hierarchy of effects model explores how promotional campaigns can progress consumers through various stages, from awareness to action. This study will also be guided by the resource-based view (RBV) of the firm, which posits that a company’s resources and capabilities are the primary determinants of its competitive advantage and performance (Barney, 1991). Marketing professionals may apply the study’s findings to their strategies to drive organizational performance, while educators can incorporate the research in their curriculum to better equip future marketing practitioners. Policymakers, on the other hand, may use the study to understand the industry’s best practices and establish suitable legal and ethical frameworks. The personal interest in this study stems from the desire to contribute to the advancement of marketing knowledge, specifically in the context of the Nigerian brewing industry, and enhance my understanding of promotional strategies’ effectiveness and ethical implications. Summarize the following in 250 words: Ever since its initial introduction in the mid-1960s, the technology behind public facial recognition has increased exponentially in complexity and accuracy to where it is in 2023. Although the software has many positive benefits associated with it including stronger security measures, far more efficient shopping, and protection against identity theft, it comes with its fair share of costs such as the potential for data vulnerabilities or technology manipulation. Arguably its most important cost is its threat to individual and societal privacy, personal freedoms, and personal rights. Utilized all around the world by many countries, including the United States, in a variety of different contexts, China is undoubtedly the country with a facial recognition system that is the most pervasive in society, with a huge database of faces. In China, public facial recognition allows access to certain types of private information, which can be used to maintain a semblance of control over the general public, however, it can also be used to protect their livelihoods. 
One example of its use in China is Beijing’s Temple of Heaven installing face scanners to catch toilet paper thieves. In China many public restrooms aren’t equipped with toilet paper, however, Beijing’s Temple of Heaven was one of the few places where there was toilet paper available for patrons to use. In an attempt to curb the theft from the building, facial scanners were installed to only supply patrons with limited supplies. This has caused complaints from many people, stating that the quantity isn’t enough and also that it’s too slow as it takes around 30 seconds to fully print out the paper (Andrews, 2021). A second example of this surveillance is found in many public schools, where cameras have been installed above the blackboards whose sole purpose is to monitor a student’s facial expressions. Every 30 seconds the cameras feed the data to a machine-learning model that analyzes the facial expressions and determines whether the student is focused or not (Chan, 2018). It then sends this information to the professor and the professor grades them per the results that are returned. Not only does the system take in facial expressions, but it also monitors students’ actions and functions as a replacement for student IDs as students can buy things in the local campus store with just their faces (Tone, 2022).
These are only two examples of the advancements that China has made with its facial recognition system, but between 2010 and 2018, the number of face scanners installed in China grew by over 800% (Tone, 2022).  This ever-expanding increase in its usage raises and highlights a myriad of ethical concerns. According to G2, a peer-to-peer review site, the top six ethical concerns related to these systems in the US are racial bias due to testing inaccuracies, racial discrimination in law enforcement, data privacy, lack of informed consent and transparency, mass surveillance, and data breaches and ineffective legal support (Gangarapu, 2022). Although these considerations were written with the US in mind, all six of these can be translated into the ethical issues in China’s case. While some are more direct, such as mass surveillance and data privacy issues, others take on a different meaning. For example, while racial discrimination in law enforcement in the US mostly disadvantages African Americans, in China the software is being used to discriminate against Uighur Muslims. On the counterargument side, there are benefits to this massive increase, namely protection against identity theft and security, that should be weighed against the cost to ethically examine the issue at hand. Overall, public facial recognition can bring positive and negative effects to society which becomes a complex ethical issue that can be analyzed from different perspectives such as Deontology, Utilitarianism, and Virtue Ethics. 
Beginning with deontology, it is mainly associated with Immanuel Kant who bases the correctness of actions on fulfilling the duties of the individual performing such actions (Taylor. R.M, 2013). Therefore, by understanding the duties of the people performing facial recognition on a large scale; deontological ethics can help us understand the ethical implications of China's use of facial recognition technology. Such analysis must determine if the use of facial recognition adheres to the categorical imperative, the formula of humanity, the universalizability principle, and the overall moral worth of actions. 
From a deontological perspective, the formula of humanity states that individuals have inherent value and dignity, and they should be treated as ends in themselves, rather than as mere means to achieve some other goal (Kant, 1993). The use of facial recognition technology in public places such as airports, train stations, and shopping malls in China may be considered a violation of this principle since it treats individuals as mere means to achieve security and surveillance objectives (Dou. E, 2021). Facial recognition technology invades individuals' privacy by tracking their movements and activities in public places, without their consent or knowledge. Therefore, individuals are not being treated as autonomous agents capable of making their own decisions and living their lives autonomously. Instead, they are being monitored and controlled by the state, which undermines their dignity and freedom. 
Additionally, the use of such technology in public places in China may be considered unethical due to the idea of categorical imperatives. According to Kant, an action is good only if it conforms with a maxim that should be unquestionably universalized (Kant, 1993). In other words, an action is ethical as long as it follows rules that can become a universal law. China's use of facial recognition technology violates this principle because if it were to become a universal law, it would result in a world where everyone is constantly under surveillance, with no privacy or freedom.
Furthermore, facial recognition technology poses ethical concerns regarding the risk of bias and discrimination, as the accuracy of the system is not equal for all individuals, with higher error rates for people with darker skin tones and women (Mozur. P, 2019). From a deontological perspective, the use of facial recognition in law enforcement and security contexts may perpetuate existing biases and discrimination against certain groups of people. This issue is exacerbated by China's use of facial recognition technology, as the government has utilized the system to monitor and suppress the Uighur Muslim minority in Xinjiang province (Mozur. P, 2019). This kind of use of facial recognition technology further violates the categorical imperative, as it creates a moral dilemma wherein one cannot imagine the maxim of such an action becoming a universal law. Moreover, such utilization of facial recognition lacks moral worth because the action is not performed from a sense of duty, which is the necessity of acting from respect for the moral law. Instead, the action is performed for the purpose of improving security measures in China. Finally, the arbitrary detention and persecution of individuals based on their identity, as enabled by facial recognition technology, is a clear violation of the formula of humanity as it treats the victims as means to achieve better security measures. 
In addition to the categorical imperative and formula of humanity, deontological ethics dictates that actions should be judged based on their adherence to moral principles, rather than their outcomes. Kant describes a duty as the necessity of respecting the law; therefore, actions with moral worth must always adhere to the law regardless of its purpose. However, China's use of facial recognition technology is a prime example of actions that lack respect for the law. This is largely due to the lack of transparency and accountability in the deployment of the technology. Additionally, the lack of transparency around how this technology is used and who has access to it undermines the principle of transparency and accountability which are crucial in modern justice systems. These actions lack moral worth simply because they do not adhere to fundamental ethical principles and prioritize the interests of the state over the rights and dignity of the individual. Ultimately, a balance must be struck between security and privacy for facial recognition to be deployed; such balance must be achieved by adhering to moral principles and respecting humanity by treating Chinese citizens as ends in themselves. 

While deontology focuses on the actions themselves, utilitarianism cares more about the consequences of said actions. In its purest form, act utilitarianism operates under the simple principle that actions should produce the greatest good for the greatest number of people no matter what it takes to commit those actions. A modified form of utilitarianism that takes into account the idea that sometimes the action associated with the greatest good is extremely corrupt or immoral is rule utilitarianism. Under this framework, actions seek to follow general rules that produce the greatest good for the greatest number. The ideal of the greatest good for the greatest number can be measured in terms of the utility associated with outcomes, i.e. the total satisfaction or value of the benefits subtracted by the value of costs for outcomes. In the context of China, weighing the ethicality of their FRT systems requires weighing its perceived benefits, mainly increased safety, against its perceived costs, such as invasion of privacy and rights.
Those following the ideals of act utilitarianism would unequivocally support China’s use of public facial recognition technology as its benefits outweigh the costs in terms of citizen utility. Ironically, utilitarianism ideals have been part of the backbone of the decision-making process for the Chinese government following World II. For instance, the Lowy Institute, an independent foreign policy think-tank based out of Australia, states that “late Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping replaced dogmatic Maoism with pragmatic utilitarianism…(for) one objective - economic growth” (Yu, 2018) when he came to power in 1978. From there, “utilitarianism created China’s economic euphoria, and with it the delusion that it may surpass fundamental human moral challenges”. Although the idea may not be as ever-present under Xi Jinping’s orthodox communist regime, utilitarian ideals certainly pervaded its way into Chinese society, especially in the form of helping to make the country better, no matter the cost to its citizens.
 As aforementioned, FRT in China is mainly used as a form of state surveillance, as it “races to become the first to implement a pervasive system of algorithmic surveillance” (Diamond and Mitchell, 2018). One example of the way they seek to achieve this is by developing a “citizen-score” to incentivize good behavior through a series of cameras. With an invasion of privacy at its costs, it comes with the benefit of deterring citizens from stealing, breaking traffic laws, murdering, selling drugs, or committing other petty or serious crimes. Society as a whole would be better off with this change under act utilitarianism, where the ends justify the means, as the citizen score helps keep citizens safe without them even having to think about it. For a hypothetical case of the citizen score in action, consider “a 17-year-old teenage boy (walking) into a liquor store” to buy beer with a fake ID (Carzo, 2010). Currently, in the United States, this is a scenario that happens far too often and easily, as fake IDs become more realistic. However, in a situation such as the one China is in the process of implementing, instantly “an FRT system…alert(s) the clerk behind the counter”, making it impossible for the boy to buy alcohol and thus making the world as a whole safer. FRT’s positive consequences are the prevention of the child breaking the law, preventing the “potential over-consumption of alcohol”, and improving the happiness of those close to him by keeping him safe, all with an associated cost of decreased privacy. 
Rule utilitarianism’s perspective on China’s increasing FRT usage holds a similar opinion to act utilitarianism with a caveat. The main difference between the set ethical theories is that while rule utilitarianism always seeks the greatest good for the greatest number, individuals must also commit actions limited by a general code of conduct. For example, consider two Chinese citizens A and B. A murders B in broad daylight in the middle of a city street and using their widespread facial recognition technology, A is caught on the other side of the city and arrested for him. Under both act and rule utilitarianism, this would be an acceptable use of the technology as it was used to prevent a potential serial killer from murdering again without violating a code of conduct. Now consider the toilet paper theft example. Green Air (GA) is the second-largest airline in the United Kingdom. Beginning with a fleet of only 12 planes, the firm has grown to a fleet of 272 planes and travels to an impressive 191 destinations. In addition, GA was a founding member of the OneStar alliance in 1997, when it decided to work closely with four other worldwide airlines.
Historically, GA was seen as a highly appealing job that provided competitive pay and benefits, particularly when compared to other UK airlines. However, the growth of the business in the United Kingdom, as well as increased worldwide rivalry, has altered the nature of work and leadership strategy. Nonetheless, GA has a dedicated client base and is one of the most recognised UK companies.

Overview of HR issues:
Staff acted in 2005 when the contracts of 780 employees were not extended, and they were replaced with agency employees. Strike action was narrowly avoided in 2007 as the corporation reversed suggestions for pay freezes. Although these issues were formally settled, they appear to have had a long-term detrimental influence on employee morale and public perception. In 2018, a strike was called in reaction to poor working conditions for flight attendants.
Flight attendants have always worked in a defined group or team, with the same contracts and awards. However, to be more flexible, several flights began using’ mixed fleet crews,’ which meant that flight attendants were frequently working with different colleagues with different tenure and, as it turned out, separate employment contracts. Prior to 2015, employees were discovered to be on contracts with substantially better remuneration packages and shift arrangements. According to Unite the Union, some flight attendants employed after 2015 on newer contracts are on ‘poverty wages,’ with many sleeping in their cars between shifts and struggling to afford gasoline, housing fees, and food. Another concern has been the rigorous sick policy imposed on all flight attendants. Employees do not receive sick pay over the legal minimum. Because they cannot afford to take time off without compensation, flight attendants have been forced to work while unwell. The strike action launched in 2018 did not settle these concerns and is one of the longest ongoing contentious in recent times in the UK.
There is also a broader issue of low morale within the firm. Even though many of the conflicts have been resolved, employees continue to express unhappiness in the most recent annual employee survey. Sick leave policies, a lack of authority over working hours, and poor compensation are listed as major motivators. Another issue that the leadership team has noticed is the company’s negative public impression. Many consumers have complained about extended delays, bad service, and a lack of customer assistance. Category Instructions: Dealership Discussion
The purpose of the category Dealership Discussion is to determine what the caller is discussing with the dealership.

Helpful information:
Connected calls:
Calls must be considered connected to be reviewed in this category. If the call does not qualify as connected, the correction option should be selected to remove the call from the category. A call is considered connected when the caller has either reached the desired agent or reached a qualified agent that can assist the caller.
Qualified agent:
A qualified agent is an employee that can assist a caller with most or all of his or her inquiry. The qualified agent may at times be too busy to handle the inquiry at the time of the call, or he or she may need to gather more information and call back to provide an answer or solution. These scenarios are still considered connected to a qualified agent if the same agent is the one intending to return the call.
Unqualified agent:
An unqualified agent is an employee that is not able to assist the caller with most or all of his or her inquiry either during that specific call or in a promised follow-up call from the same agent.
Interactive systems and auto-attendants:
Calls handled by an interactive system or auto-attendant will sound like interactive recordings that ask questions or request information and require the caller to interact by making phone selections. These can be either Connected or Not Connected.
When a call is successfully handled by an interactive system or auto-attendant it should be considered a connected call, and proper review selections should be made according to the content and outcome of the call.
When a caller leaves a call back number with the interactive system, instead of successfully handling their inquiry or need, then the call should be considered not connected.
Here are the options:
Opportunity to buy/sell/lease/trade a vehicle
Call represented an opportunity for the dealership to buy, sell, lease, or trade a vehicle
The call does not have to include the mention of a particular make or model.
Some opportunities to buy, sell, lease, or trade may at times only mention vehicle specs. These should be listened to carefully to determine if there is an opportunity for the dealership to buy, sell, lease, or trade a vehicle.
All calls that include a caller's interest in buying, selling, leasing, or trading a vehicle should be reviewed with this option, even if the vehicle is not currently available.
Caller inquiries about a vehicle of interest
This may include but is not limited to inquiries about vehicles seen online, in an advertisement, or from driving past the dealership's lot.
Caller expresses general interest in vehicle inventory
This may include but is not limited to inquiries regarding what vehicles are available that fit the caller's price range or what vehicles meet certain desired criteria.
Call is about payment or financing options for the purchase of a vehicle
This does not include calls regarding the financing of a vehicle that is already in the caller's possession.
Caller is inquiring about leasing a vehicle or is interested in a lease buyout
Caller would like to sell or trade a vehicle to the dealership
Caller is another dealership that represents an opportunity to buy or sell a vehicle
This does not include conversations about dealer trades. Dealer trades are not opportunities for a dealership to buy or sell a vehicle. Dealer trades, sometimes also referred to as dealer swaps, are when competing dealerships trade cars with each other, swapping similar cars to meet the demands of their customers. These are exchanges of vehicles only, and they do not represent buying or selling.
Service / parts / collision / body shop
Call is regarding automotive service
This may include but is not limited to service department hour inquiries, general service questions, service needs, service appointments, or inquiring about the status of a vehicle that is already being serviced by the dealership.
Call is regarding automotive parts
This may include but is not limited to parts department hour inquiries, general parts questions, part orders, or price and installation inquiries.
Call is regarding automotive collision or the body shop
This may include but is not limited to collision or body shop department hour inquiries, general collision or body shop questions, price and repair inquiries, and collision or body shop appointments.
General / caller not in market / dealer trade
Caller has general questions or a general conversation that does not represent an opportunity for the buying, selling, or trading of a vehicle
Caller is inquiring about the status of a vehicle order that has already been placed
Caller is inquiring about the delivery of a vehicle they have already purchased
Caller is from a transport company delivering a vehicle or multiple vehicles
Call is about financing and there was no opportunity for the buying, selling, or trading of a vehicle
Call is about the refinancing of a vehicle that is already in the caller's possession
Call is about the payments for a vehicle that is already in the caller's possession
Caller only states that they are coming to the dealership to drop off paperwork, payment, or another item but they do not specify what the drop off is for
Unless a caller specifies that the drop off is regarding an opportunity to buy, sell, lease, or trade a vehicle, or that the drop off is for the service, parts, collision, or body shop departments, then we cannot assume what the drop off is regarding and the call should be considered general.
Call is about the renewal of an existing lease
Call is about the rental of a vehicle or a loaner car
Caller is inquiring about a warranty, tags, or plates
Caller only asks about hours of operation for the business and does not specify a department of service, parts, collision, or body shop
If a caller specifies the sales department, but they only ask about hours of operation for the sales department, it does not represent an opportunity for the buying, selling, or trading of a vehicle and should be considered a general call.
Caller is returning a missed call but the call ends with neither caller nor business identifying the original caller or reason for the call
If a caller's sole inquiry is to identify the reason for a missed call, and they are told by the answering agent that the original caller or reason for the call cannot be identified, this is considered enough information to satisfy the caller's reason for calling. The caller needs no further information, nor needs any further connection to any agent or employee. Thus, the answering agent is qualified, and the call is considered handled.
Caller is returning a missed call but is not in the market to buy, sell, trade, or lease a vehicle
This will often sound like an agent asking a caller if he or she is interested in buying, selling, leasing, or trading in a vehicle, and the caller informing the agent that he or she is not in the market.
Calls should only be considered opportunities when the caller is in the market, regardless of if the agent mentioned a specific vehicle or attempted to encourage the caller to buy, sell, lease, or trade a vehicle. When callers are not in the market, they do not represent business opportunities for the dealership.
Call is regarding a dealer trade
Dealer trades are not opportunities for a dealership to buy or sell a vehicle. Dealer trades, sometimes also referred to as dealer swaps, are when competing dealerships trade cars with each other, swapping similar cars to meet the demands of their customers. These are exchanges of vehicles only, and they do not represent buying or selling.
Caller is from a third-party company asking for information about a vehicle that a mutual customer is interested in
Calls from a third-party company, such as a finance company, may request vehicle information for their own business needs regarding the mutual customer. These third-party companies are not customers, and therefore should not be considered an opportunity to buy, sell, lease, or trade a vehicle.
Caller only refers someone to the dealership but does not themself represent an opportunity for the caller to buy, sell, lease, or trade a vehicle
A referrer alone is not the customer. They are solely attempting to provide the dealership with information about a potential customer. A call should only be considered an opportunity to buy, sell, lease, or trade a vehicle once the actual customer and dealership connect.
Call is an agent-to-agent discussion about a mutual customer but does not represent an opportunity to buy, sell, lease, or trade a vehicle on behalf of the customer
Agent-to-agent discussions, regarding internal business for the dealership, do not themselves represent opportunities.
A call should only be considered an opportunity to buy, sell, lease, or trade a vehicle when the actual customer is the one involved in the discussion with dealership or when the agent involved is speaking on behalf of the customer with the intent to buy, sell, lease, or trade a vehicle.

Unqualified agent: An employee that is not able to assist the caller with his or her inquiry. A caller may reach an unqualified employee and hold a conversation, but it is not considered a connected call unless the caller is connected to someone who can assist him or her with their inquiry.
Appointment opportunity: Connected calls about potential maintenance or repair service(s) the shop can perform, repair or installation of a part that the shop can perform, or confirmed open recalls that the service shop can perform.
Service opportunities include but are not limited to:
Oil changes
Fluid flushes
Key programming / key cutting / key battery replacement
Part installation
Tire installation
Battery installation
Car detailing
Call types that should NOT be considered service:
Body work or collision repair
Car washes
Finance, sales, etc.
Interactive systems and auto-attendants: Calls handled by an interactive system or auto-attendant will sound like interactive recordings that ask questions or request information and require the caller to interact by making phone selections. When a call is successfully handled by an interactive system or auto-attendant it should be considered a connected call, and proper review selections should be made according to the content and outcome of the call. When a caller leaves a call back number with the interactive system, instead of successfully handling their inquiry or need, then the call should be considered not connected.

Caller agrees to an appointment with a specific date and time.

Caller approximates a loose time range, but the agent puts down a firm time for the appointment. In these instances, the agent’s statement trumps the caller's.

Caller agrees to an approximate time within a 1 hour time range because they are able to be serviced at the time of arrival.
A walk-in time within an hour range, for a vehicle that can be serviced immediately, should be considered a specific appointment time. Example call - Caller: "I need to get my brakes repaired. Do you have any openings today?"// Agent: "You can come in now if you'd like"// Caller: "Great! I'll be there in half an hour." // Call ends.

Caller agrees to an approximate time of "around 1 hour".

Caller gives a vague agreement to possibly come in.

Caller agrees to come in but approximates a time range that exceeds 1 hour.

Slide 2 & 3: Introduction

- Brief introduction of adidas

Adidas AG, a multinational corporation founded in Germany in 1949, is one of the world’s leading sportswear, footwear, and equipment manufacturers. It is the second-largest sportswear manufacturer globally, after Nike. The company was founded by Adolf Dassler, the brother of Rudolf Dassler, who eventually started Puma, another popular sportswear brand. The brand, known for its signature three-stripe logo, has grown to become a significant player in the global sports industry, with products catering to professional athletes, sports teams, and individuals seeking high-quality performance apparel, footwear, and accessories. Adidas has its global headquarters in Herzogenaurach, Germany, and employs over 60,000 people globally. Adidas has a long and illustrious history in the sports and fashion industries. The brand’s logo is iconic, consisting of three parallel stripes that represent strength, speed, and endurance. The stripes were originally added to sports shoes to provide greater stability but were soon incorporated into the brand’s identity.

Adidas operates under a mission “to be the best sports company in the world.” It illustrates this by maintaining innovative product designs, using advanced technologies, and investing in sustainability initiatives. In addition to its core adidas brand, the company also owns Reebok and has forged numerous partnerships with top athletes, sports teams, and leading designers across various sectors.

- Overview of the presentation’s objectives
The goal of this presentation is to delve into the adidas brand’s DNA to understand its values, voice, triumphs, and setbacks. By critically analyzing adidas’ brand value proposition, market positioning, customer perception, and emerging market trends, we will gain insight into the brand’s current state and identify opportunities for growth. Building on this analysis, the presentation will introduce a new sub-brand idea with a clear value proposition and future positioning strategy, supported by evidence and trends.

The presentation will cover the following objectives:
1. To critically review the current adidas brand value proposition
2. To critically discuss the market positioning of adidas
3. To critically evaluate customer perception of adidas
4. To investigate emerging market trends that adidas could capitalize on
5. To introduce a new sub-brand idea, including key value proposition and future positioning

- Importance of brand management for businesses
Effective brand management is crucial for any business, as it helps shape customer perceptions and sets the foundation for robust relationships between a brand and its customers. A well-managed brand can help a company stand out from competitors, strengthen its market position, and drive growth.

Meanwhile, a poorly managed brand can harm a company’s reputation, diminish customer loyalty, and hinder its ability to compete effectively in the market. As a global brand, adidas must continually monitor, evaluate, and refine its brand management strategies to ensure it remains at the forefront of the sports industry and meets its customers’ evolving needs and preferences.

In sum, our comprehensive analysis of the adidas brand will provide valuable insights to help the company further enhance its brand value, market position, and customer engagement, ultimately supporting the mission of becoming the best sports company in the world.

Slides 4-6 : Brand Heritage 

- Overview of the adidas brand’s historical development
Adidas, founded by Adolf “Adi” Dassler in 1949, has a rich history rooted in innovation, quality, and a passion for sports. Its origins date back to the 1920s when Adi Dassler and his brother Rudolf started a shoe company, Gebrüder Dassler Schuhfabrik, in their mother’s laundry room. The brothers’ innovative sports shoes gained recognition at the 1936 Olympics, where Jesse Owens wore them while winning four gold medals.

However, disagreements between the two brothers led to the dissolution of their partnership, and Adi Dassler formed adidas while Rudolf established PUMA. The iconic three-stripe logo made its debut on adidas shoes in 1949, and the brand continued to gain fame through endorsements with prominent athletes and national teams.

Over the decades, adidas has evolved and diversified its product offerings, targeting various sports categories, including running, football, basketball, and training. The acquisition of Reebok in 2006 reinforced the company’s position in the sports market, and partnerships with designers such as Yohji Yamamoto and Stella McCartney added a high-fashion dimension to the brand.

- Key milestones in the adidas brand’s evolution
1. 1949: Adi Dassler establishes adidas and introduces the three-stripe logo.
2. 1954: The German national football team wins the World Cup wearing adidas’ screw-in stud shoes, further bolstering the brand’s reputation in sports innovation.
3. 1970: Adidas becomes the official ball supplier for the FIFA World Cup.
4. 1980s-1990s: The brand expands from sports shoes into the broader sportswear and equipment market, including apparel, accessories, and sports equipment.
5. 2006: Acquisition of Reebok bolsters the adidas Group’s presence within North America and strengthens its position in the global sports market.
6. 2010s: Continued expansion of adidas’ product offerings, with notable partnerships including Y-3 with Yohji Yamamoto, collaboration with Kanye West on Yeezy, and partnerships with high-profile athletes such as Lionel Messi and James Harden.
7. 2015: Introduction of the Parley for the Oceans initiative, showcasing adidas’ commitment to sustainability by using ocean plastic waste to create performance footwear and apparel.
8. 2020: Adidas announces a partnership with Allbirds, another sustainability-focused footwear brand, aimed at creating the lowest carbon footprint sports shoe possible.

- The adidas brand’s mission, values, and beliefs
Adidas’ mission is to be the best sports company in the world, expressing this through the brand’s three-pillar strategy: Speed, Key Cities, and Open Source. These pillars aim to foster innovation, focus on crucial urban markets, and encourage collaboration among athletes, consumers, and partners.

The brand seeks to empower people through sports by adhering to its core values – passion, integrity, innovation, and teamwork. These values are reflected in numerous initiatives, including sustainable product design, inclusive sizing and representation in campaigns, and investments in employee development and well-being.

Adidas is a brand that believes in the transformative power of sports, working tirelessly to create products and experiences that enable people to harness this power and improve their lives.

- Visual representation using elements of the brand heritage model
An effective framework for examining adidas’ brand heritage is Keller’s Brand System Model. It comprises four components
1. Brand Identity (Adidas Logo and Three-Stripe Mark): Adidas’ iconic logo, featuring three stripes, represents the unity, quality, and performance associated with the brand.
2. Brand Meaning (Innovation, Quality, and Passion for Sports): The key elements of adidas’ brand meaning include innovation in sports equipment and apparel, high-quality products, and a genuine love for sports in all forms.
3. Brand Response (Customer Loyalty, Recognition, and Emotion): Adidas elicits strong responses from consumers, including loyalty, recognition of the brand and its values, and emotional connections to sports, performance, and self-improvement.
4. Brand Relationship (Athletes, Teams, Designers, and Partnerships): Adidas has cultivated robust relationships with professional athletes, sports teams, designers, and partners, fostering collaboration and contributing to the brand’s continued growth and relevance.

Introduction

The research topic that will be explored in this study is the role of social media in music preference among Gen Z, a demographic group born between 1997 and 2012.   The rise of social media platforms have brought immense changes in the way people connect, share and express their interests. As digital natives, Gen Z has grown up with social media and their experiences with music are likely to be different than previous generations. According to a report by Nielsen Music, over 80% of Gen Z listens to music on YouTube, and social media platforms like Instagram, Twitter, and TikTok have become a crucial tool for artists to promote their music and engage with their fan base (NME, 2020). Social media platforms provide ample opportunities for users to explore, discover, and share music that reflects their personal preferences. 

Previously, music promotion was done through radio, television or physical sales, but now social media platforms and streaming services have taken over.When we talk about the significance of this topic both theoretically and socio-economically, we need to understand the impact of a music genre on the society and vice versa. The theoretical significance of this research is to understand how social media platforms shape the identity formation, as well as the cultural and social communication of music, amongst Gen Z individuals. By exploring the impact of social media on music preference, and using Social Cognitive theory, this research can further provide insight into how social media is influencing the music industry.

Literature review
Existing research consistently highlights the significance of social media in the music discovery process for younger generations (Datta et al., 2017; Baym, 2017). For example, Datta et al. (2017) found that the adoption of online streaming significantly affects music consumption and discovery among listeners.

Literature has also explored the role of peer networks and online influencers on music preferences (Martínez-Castaño et al., 2016; Marwick, 2015). Martínez-Castaño et al. (2016) suggest that social media strategies, including the use of online influencers, can effectively promote indie music to listeners.

While there is a growing body of literature on the role of social media in music preferences, few studies have specifically focused on Gen Z (Datta et al., 2017), who have grown up with social media as a central aspect of their lives. 

Additionally, current literature does not fully address the complex and varying ways in which social media interacts with and influences individual listening habits and taste development. 

This research aims to address these gaps by focusing on the music preferences of Gen Z in relation to social media use.

1. Existing literature suggests that social media has a significant impact on music preferences among young adults. Strong evidence suggests that social media platforms such as Spotify, YouTube, and TikTok are the most popular sources of music for Gen Z population (Cicchetti, 2022). However, there is a lack of research on how and to what extent social media specifically influences music preferences.

2. The research on social media’s effect on music preferences has shown a positive relationship between social media use and musical taste formation (Meehan, 2019). Moreover, research suggests that social media can be an integral tool for music discovery and sharing amongst young adults and can play a role in shaping the music industry (Webster, 2021).

3. Research on the impact of social media on music preferences suggests that social media allows for the creation of alternative music genres and subcultures that appeal to younger individuals (Güven, 2016). However, there is a gap in the literature in the study of how these genres and subcultures come into existence and what role social media plays in their formation.

4. Various studies have also highlighted how social media contributes to the development of music fandoms, and the impact of fandoms on the music industry (Derbaix & Korchia, 2019). However, there is still a lack of understanding of how social media creates fan communities, and if these fan communities are influenced by social media algorithms.

5. Research has shown that social media can lead to a phenomenon known as "musical convergence” (Vizcaíno-Verdú et al., 2023). Musical convergence occurs when individuals begin to share common musical tastes due to the influence of social media algorithms. However, the extent to which social media algorithms play a role in the formation of musical preferences is still not fully understood.

6. Existing literature suggests that social media platforms can create a sense of community for individuals with niche musical interests (Sharabati et al., 2022). However, there is a lack of understanding on how social media facilitates human interaction within these communities.

7. The existing literature has identified several challenges related to social media’s impact on music preferences, among which is the lack of diversity in the music that is promoted through social media algorithms (Elliott & Reynolds, 2019). This research highlights the importance of exploring how social media can contribute to diversity in music preference.

Existing literature suggests that social media has a significant impact on music preference among the younger population. However, there is still a lack of understanding of how and to what extent social media influences music preference among Gen Z. The above-discussed gap in the literature justifies the need for research to investigate the role of social media in shaping the music preference of Gen Z. While there is a growing body of literature on the role of social media in music preferences, few studies have specifically focused on Gen Z 
(Cohen & Rosenbaum, 2014), who have grown up with social media as a central aspect of their lives. This research aims to address these gaps by focusing on the music preferences of Gen Z in relation to social media use.

Research Questions

The major research question for this study is: What is the role of social media in shaping the music preferences of Gen Z?

Minor questions include:
• What specific social media platforms are most influential in shaping music preferences among Gen Z?
• How do peer networks and online influencers contribute to the development of music preferences among Gen Z?
• To what extent does exposure to diverse genres and artists through social media impact music taste development among Gen Z?

Methods
The research design will be a mixed-methods approach, incorporating both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis. This will allow for a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the relationship between social media use and music preferences among Gen Z.

Quantitative data analysis: Descriptive statistics and inferential statistics will be used to analyze the quantitative data from the questionnaires. This will include computing frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations to explore relationships between variables of interest, such as social media use and music preferences.

Throughout the Victorian period, extending from 1837 to 1901, England underwent considerable socio-cultural transformations, particularly in the context of the Industrial Revolution. As Peter Coveney writes, “the child was at the heart of his interests, at the centre of the Dickens world. He utilised the child perspective as a mechanism for scrutinising the duplicity, injustice, and somber realities of Victorian society through the unblemished lens of a child, bearing witness to these phenomena as firsthand experiences. Children thus began to engage with society critically, contradicting the prevailing notion that they would simply absorb, imitate, and adhere to adult perspectives.
Scholarly discourse regarding the use of child narrators in adult literature commonly attributes the inception of this technique to Mark Twain’s renowned work, The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884). According to the translation of Schneider Helena’s work by Linda Steinmetz, Twain’s Huckleberry Finn holds the distinction of being the first literary composition that consistently renders a child’s perspective throughout the entire narrative. However, Charles Dickens did not undertake any extensive literary exploration in his novels to present a continuous and comprehensive representation of the world as perceived by children. Rather, he opted for a technique that involved amalgamating an adult narrative voice with the recounted viewpoint of a child character. In David Copperfield, the eponymous protagonist’s bildungsroman unfolds as a retrospective narrative, imbuing the text with a duality that intersects juvenile naivete and critical adult scrutiny. The narrative oscillates between the liminal spaces of innocence and experience, manifesting Dickens’ depth of characterization and his ontological exploration of the multifaceted progression of human consciousness. The child narrator’s voice construes a dialectical tension between the internal and external worlds, accentuating the verisimilitude of diverse emotional responses vis-a-vis the protagonist’s evolving social landscape. For instance, David’s relationship with the sadistic Mr. Murdstone and the gruelling experiences at the industrial boarding school expose readers to the harsh realities of the Victorian era, implicating themes such as poverty, child labour, and cruelty in a deeply personal manner. This remarkable skill allows him to effectively bridge the gap between past and present, and to offer a nuanced and insightful perspective on the human experience. By tapping into his own memories and utilizing his adult intellect, David is able to create a rich and compelling portrait of childhood that effectively captures the complexity and depth of this formative period in his life. As Mark Spilka observes, “the childlike view connects unconscious tensions with the conscious scene. Again in Great Expectations, Pip’s first-person narrative voice presents a bildungsroman imbued with a child’s wonder and confusion. Pip, the protagonist, serves as both the focalizer and the narrator of the story, employing the pronoun “I” to convey his thoughts, feelings, and perceptions. Nonetheless, the novel’s narrative structure incorporates two distinct versions of the protagonist’s self, which are demarcated by their temporal and experiential differences between them. The adult Pip, endowed with a more mature and informed perspective, serves as the overt narrator of the story. At the same time, the child Pip, who is characterized by his emotional and intuitive nature, represents the implied narrator, whose voice is subtly integrated into the narrative. The narrative skillfully maintains a delicate balance between Pip’s childish perspective, which encompasses feelings of “terror, fascination, and helplessness,” and the perspective of the mature narrator, who appears “confident, secure, and powerful in his recollection of the event.” (Jordan p. 78)
Thus both David Copperfield and Great Expectations employ retrospective narratives to construct vivid and multi-layered portrayals of their protagonists’ journeys of self-discovery. The duality between the protagonist’s past and present selves offers a rich exploration of the human psyche, highlighting the interplay between unconscious tensions and conscious experience. The main advantage of using the dual narratives of a child and an adult (experiencing self and the narrating self) not only enhances the reader’s understanding but also preserves the distinctiveness of Pip and David, which is essential to the development of the novels’ plots. Indeed, for a larger part, these characters are not afforded the opportunity to enter into the minds of others but are instead endowed with a remarkable ability to recall and articulate their own emotions and observations. (Brown p. 198) In this regard, Dickens’ literary technique in his works, as mentioned above, presents a stark contrast to Mark Twain’s approach in The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. Twain’s novel is remarkable in giving an unadulterated and uninterrupted portrayal of a child’s perspective throughout the text, providing an authentic representation of a child’s cognitive, emotional, and social development.
Mark Twain’s Huckleberry Finn unarguably stands as a tour de force in the realm of American Literature, exemplifying a skillfully crafted bildungsroman embedded within a broader social commentary. Set against the meandering backdrop of the Mississippi River, the tale unfolds an odyssey of self-discovery and moral evolution for the eponymous protagonist as he grapples with the prevailing ethical codes and societal norms of his epoch. The novel’s narrative voice unfurls through the first-person perspective of a child narrator (Huck), whose innocence and rustic charm offer a unique window into the complexities and contradictions inherent in the nineteenth-century American South. Situated within this somber context, we find an elaborate microcosm of child relations (Huck and Jim; Huck and Buck, etc.) intricately interlaced in such an emotionally and intellectually captivating manner that it seizes the reader’s focus, compelling them to rethink–in accordance with Barry Marks’ assertions–the inherent essence of “truth and the possibility of open and sincere human relationships.” (The making of Humorist : the narrative strategy p. 140) As articulated by Clarence A. Brown, one of the most striking features of Mark Twain’s Huckleberry Finn is the remarkable “consistency” with which the author has crafted the “illusion” that the narrative is conveyed by the titular character, Huck himself. Right from the beginning of the work, Twain unambiguously positions Huck as the narrative’s focal point – the “center of consciousness” or the “reflector.” Twain’s explicit narration from Huck’s perspective presents a filtered view of events, emphasising Huck’s dual role as a reporter and a center of consciousness. As a reporter, Huck accurately records what he observes, but as a center of consciousness, he “refracts” his experiences through his own imagination and viewpoint, shaping the narrative’s tone and meaning. The novel contains two distinct worlds: one that exists outside of Huck’s limited scope of experience, which he reports accurately, and another that lies within the confines of his understanding, which he can interpret and present in greater depth. The book’s manifold effects are achieved through a “simple vocabulary aided now and again by Huck’s own coinages.” (C. A. Brown pp. 11-13) Dispensing with the idea that children ought to be sheltered within the confines of their families, the protagonist is thrust into the realm of adulthood—an apotheosis that signifies the merging of innocence and maturity. Huck could be said, in the words of Valerie Vogrin (2003), to offer the reader an “experience of the world through his eyes and ears and nose and skin.” (80) Basically, the novel’s tension and irony are generated by the interplay between the picaresque realm embarked upon by Huckleberry Finn and the convoluted adult world that engulfs him while he struggles to fathom its intricacies.

The study of child narrators and focalisers has become increasingly popular in recent years. This can be observed in the growing number of publications and scholarly works that have emerged, highlighting the growing desire to comprehend and explore the unique and nuanced perspectives of young individual. One of the key reasons for this growing interest in children’s perspectives is the recognition of the unique and valuable insights that children can offer. Today, children are no longer seen as just miniature adults or predominantly innocent or naive creatures but as “knowing, manipulative, destructive, and sexual beings.” (childhood in the contemporary novel DINTER) Instead of adhering to a linear narrative of childhood as a progression from “innocence to experience, from ignorance to knowledge, and from dependency to autonomy,” contemporary research emphasises how “childhood is shaped by the power dynamics of the generational order.” (Dinter and Schneider, 36) Modern works of literature break away from the traditional ideas of childhood as simply a stage of life. Instead, they delve into the factors, motivations, and struggles that shape its cultural creation. (Dinter, Introduction, 2020)

It is our hope that this presentation at ASSC26 will contribute to, and enrich this debate by not only elucidating the specific subjective effects, but also inspiring better phenomenological methods in the study of non-ordinary states. ASSC is attended by some of the most influential researchers and philosophers in the study of consciousness, many with an interest in how non-ordinary consciousness can inform our understanding of ordinary consciousness, and so it is an ideal forum for disseminating this work. A preliminary version of these same results were presented by James to a psychedelic-specific audience in a poster at the Interdisciplinary Conference on Psychedelic Research (ICPR) in September 2022.
Because James’ PhD program has not yet commenced (expected commencement: fall 2023), it is outside the established policies for the Centre for Psychedelic Research to fund James’ attendance at the conference. Presentation abstract——
Title:
Towards a micro-phenomenology of the intravenous DMT state
Introduction: 
When administered in the lab, the 5-HT2A receptor agonist N, N-Dimethyltryptamine (DMT) radically alters the subjective character of experience. However, scientific understanding of DMT experiences in a lab setting is limited by the shortcomings of commonly used phenomenological methods. Specifically, phenomenological models based on self-report questionnaire methods typically do not typically capture the temporal dynamics of experience, instead averaging subjective properties over the entire experience. Qualitative methods, such as thematic or content analysis, suffer this same limitation. The micro-phenomenology (MP) interview and analysis method is well suited to address this lack of granularity in psychedelic phenomenology, modelling experience richly on both the synchronic (within-moment) and diachronic (between-moments) dimensions.
Methods: 
This qualitative study is the first to apply both the MP interview and analysis method to psychedelic data. 25 participants were intravenously dosed with 20 mg of DMT fumarate in a lab setting while undergoing combined EEG and fMRI. MP interviews about the experience were performed upon return to a baseline state. A micro-phenomenological analysis protocol was applied, including novel adaptations developed to accommodate the particularities of non-ordinary experience. Synchronic and diachronic categories were extracted and used to compare and cluster similar experiences.
Results: 
A hierarchical taxonomy of categories on both the synchronic and diachronic dimensions is proposed, along with descriptions and observed frequencies of the phenomenological clusters that emerged. 
Discussion: 
In line with Varela’s ‘neurophenomenological’ research programme, further work on this project will statistically validate the phenomenological clusters identified here against the corresponding fMRI and EEG data. Additionally, the present study can be seen as the first step in a micro-phenomenological pipeline, starting here with a comprehensive look at entire DMT experiences, before narrowing down in further work to study component experiences (e.g.: the experience of presences that seem to have their own minds, colloquially referred to as ‘DMT entities’) at the micro-phenomenological level.

Automation regularly optimizes one and only one part of the business process. Hyperautomation allows a more global action than automation, on the whole process chain.

WHAT IS HYPERAUTOMATION?
Hyperautomation could be summarized as a technology or a set of technologies that will enable a more complete, agile and end-to-end automation of the organization. We can notice, among others, two main categories of technologies:

Technologies related to Artificial Intelligence with for example:
 Machine Learning: to identify, categorize and organize information with a learning logic
Deep Learning: learning technology based on artificial neurons
NLP (Natural Language Processing): that allows a machine to recognize and understand human language
 
    2. Technologies related to the automation of information systems:
BPM, which automatically maps a process and all the human/machine interactions in the company, and iBPM, which adds a first level of intelligence to BPM, such as machine learning or the automation of certain tasks called RPA

iPaaS: a platform that simplifies the integration of data, applications and systems of an enterprise in the cloud. These platforms facilitate the interconnection of your solutions and systems and allow a better fluidity and agility within the organization

Low code / No code: technologies that allow from automatic or visual models to create mobile or web applications without computer development
RPA: technologies that enable the automation of business tasks
FOR WHICH FIELDS OF APPLICATION?
Hyperautomation can be applied to a wide range of domains and global processes such as:

CUSTOMER RELATIONSHIP
Hyperautomation enables drastic cost reduction while improving the customer experience. The impact can be on improving customer journeys such as underwriting, optimizing customer processing times...
Click Here
SUPPLY CHAIN
By optimizing the entire delivery chain, for example by including the various stakeholders (supply, supply chain, delivery, etc.)
Click Here
FINANCE
Thanks to an optimization of the Order to Cash and Procure to Pay processes as a whole
Click Here
BENEFITS OF HYPERAUTOMATION
The benefits of hyperautomation are multiple and can be grouped into 3 main categories:

A benefit for your teams: Thanks to hyperautomation, your teams can now focus on tasks with higher added value, leaving aside the most repetitive and uninteresting tasks. In the context of customer relations, for example, they will be able to bring value to the most complex issues and thus deliver a better customer experience. This brings a greater capacity to respond to customers and a better operational efficiency. This will only increase their involvement and motivation

Hyperautomation will also be a real decision support tool. By processing and automating a greater number of tasks, hyperautomation will, thanks to the technologies used, capture a lot of data and knowledge about the company’s operations. This structured data constitutes a real added value for decision making in the company

Hyperautomation also allows for better compliance and risk control in the company through the control and mastery of processes operated in the field. The example of financial processes speaks for itself: by automating a greater number of tasks done by humans, the company reduces the risk of errors
 

Engaged and value-focused associates, reliable and compliant processes, as well as data for decision making, make hyperautomation a real productivity lever for the company.

PROCESS MINING: A REQUIREMENT FOR HYPERAUTOMATION?
Hyperautomation requires an accurate view of the performance of your existing processes and how they work.
Mark Kerremans, VP Analyst at Gartner, talks about the fundamental role of Process Mining in the successful implementation of hyperautomation: it provides an end-to-end view of your business processes and brings an essential understanding of the field before automating.

It allows you to model and restore a dynamic vision of how your processes are operated in real time in the field.
It visually represents bottlenecks, reworks, non-conformities etc. This way, you can easily identify the main difficulties in your processes, those that make you lose money or time.
It automatically identifies the root causes of these difficulties. Thanks to Process Mining, you can focus on a specific part of your process and explain where these anomalies come from.
Finally, it allows you to have a predictive view of your processes to better anticipate the expected results or gains if a modification of your processes were to be made.
To conclude, hyperautomation goes beyond simple automation and allows the creation of much more independent systems and processes capable of going faster, of carrying out more and more complex tasks that can even go as far as decision making.'

PART B: Assignment Description

The goal of the assignment is to have students write a public official regarding a problem that is affecting the world today. The public official nevertheless has to be a real one, but students are not obligated to send them the letter. Importantly, students will have to identify which public official they are writing.
To write the letter, students are required to use the external sources listed in Part D. They can nonetheless write about any problem within the themes listed in that section. For example, they can write about the problem of hospital wait times within the broader Health Care theme. Or, then again, they can write about Ukraine’s request for jets within the broader War in the Ukraine theme.
A model and example of how to structure such a letter will be provided in Part E of this document.
In terms of getting ideas as to who to write, students might consider bearing in mind the following. For municipal politics such as public transportation and policing; students should consider writing their city councillor or mayor. For matters relevant to provincial politics such as education, health care, and social services; students should consider writing the Member of Provincial Parliament (MPP) or the Premier of Ontario. For matters relevant to federal politics such as foreign policy and national economic policy; students should consider writing their Member of Parliament (MP) or the Prime Minister. See Part F of this document for tools for finding their elected officials. Should students want to write an official from another country, they are free to do so. Nevertheless, it will be up to them to find the appropriate contact information. 
PART C: Assignments Structure/Evaluation Scheme
The Letter to a Public Official will be evaluated accordingly:
1.	2 points will be granted for clearly and properly identifying their public official by listing their name, position, and official address at the top of the letter.
2.	3 points will be granted for indicating why (a) they are writing that official in particular (1.5 points) and (b) the purpose of the letter (1.5 points) This is where students (you) outline the problem or issue that you would like resolved or addressed. This should be between 2 to 3 sentences long. 
3.	5 Points will be granted for explaining the issue or problem students (you) would like to be addressed or resolved.* This could include identifying important actors, laws/decisions, and events. An explanation and summary of the history of the issue or problem can also be provided if possible. This paragraph should be between 4 to 8 sentences long. However, students can write more than 8 sentences in this section should they wish to.
*1 Point Students (you) will need to consult and cite at least one of the sources listed in Part D. Students can, of course, cite more than one source from that list.
4.	4 Points will be granted in total for explaining what decision the public official should make with regard to the problem or issue that the student (you) would like to be addressed or resolved. This paragraph should include both a (a) description of the decision or action they would like the official to take (2 points) and (b) an explanation (s) to justify why that decision or action should be taken (2 points). This section should be between This paragraph should be between 4 to 8 sentences long. However, students can write more than 8 sentences in this section should they wish to.
5.	2 Points will be granted for properly locating and structuring the in-text citations.
6.	2 Points will be granted for properly structuring the bibliography.
7.	1 Point will be granted for spelling and grammar
